title: Town and getting around
intro: Words for finding your way and naming what you pass. This unit has more regional variation than any other in the book — the bus alone has five names — so the alternatives are given where they matter.

entries.note: Stress on the last syllable: ciu-DAD.

ex.es: Es la ciudad más grande del país.
ex.en: It's the largest city in the country.

entries.en: village, small town; the people, the populace
entries.note: The second sense is the political one — el pueblo mexicano, the Mexican people.

ex.es: Mis abuelos viven en un pueblo pequeño.
ex.en: My grandparents live in a small village.

ex.es: El pueblo salió a la calle.
ex.en: The people took to the streets.

entries.note: Double l sounds like English y in most of Latin America; in Buenos Aires it is closer to sh.

ex.es: Vivo en la calle Bolívar.
ex.en: I live on Bolívar Street.

entries.note: Abbreviated Av. in addresses. Wider than a calle and usually numbered or named after a date.

ex.es: Camina dos cuadras por la avenida.
ex.en: Walk two blocks along the avenue.

entries.note: An outside corner where two streets meet. An inside corner of a room is el rincón.

ex.es: Nos vemos en la esquina de Juárez y Reforma.
ex.en: Let's meet at the corner of Juárez and Reforma.

entries.note: The standard unit of walking directions in Latin America. Spain says manzana.

ex.es: Está a tres cuadras de aquí.
ex.en: It's three blocks from here.

entries.note: The centre of any Latin American town, usually with a church on one side.

ex.es: La plaza se llena los domingos.
ex.en: The square fills up on Sundays.

ex.es: Los niños juegan en el parque hasta que oscurece.
ex.en: The children play in the park until it gets dark.

entries.note: A shop for a specific trade takes -ería: panadería, librería, zapatería.

ex.es: La tienda cierra a las nueve.
ex.en: The shop closes at nine.

ex.es: En el mercado todo es más barato.
ex.en: Everything is cheaper at the market.

entries.note: el colegio is also school, not college. University is la universidad.

ex.es: La escuela está frente al parque.
ex.en: The school is opposite the park.

ex.es: Lo llevaron al hospital anoche.
ex.en: They took him to the hospital last night.

entries.note: Context alone separates the two. A river bank is la orilla, a third thing entirely.

ex.es: El banco abre a las nueve.
ex.en: The bank opens at nine.

ex.es: Nos sentamos en un banco del parque.
ex.en: We sat on a park bench.

ex.es: La iglesia es del siglo XVII.
ex.en: The church is from the seventeenth century.

ex.es: Te espero en la estación.
ex.en: I'll wait for you at the station.

ex.es: Mi estación favorita es el otoño.
ex.en: My favourite season is autumn.

ex.es: El camino al río es de tierra.
ex.en: The road to the river is unpaved.

ex.es: Nos perdimos en el camino.
ex.en: We got lost on the way.

entries.note: Regional roulette: camión in Mexico, guagua in the Caribbean, colectivo in Argentina, micro in Chile, bus almost everywhere. autobús is understood by all of them.

ex.es: El autobús pasa cada veinte minutos.
ex.en: The bus comes every twenty minutes.

ex.es: Perdimos el último tren.
ex.en: We missed the last train.

entries.note: carro in Mexico, Colombia and Central America; auto in Argentina and Chile; coche in Spain. All three are understood everywhere.

ex.es: Dejé el carro en la esquina.
ex.en: I left the car on the corner.

entries.en: to drive; to handle, to manage
entries.note: Latin America drives with manejar; Spain uses conducir.

ex.es: No sé manejar.
ex.en: I don't know how to drive.

ex.es: Ella maneja muy bien la presión.
ex.en: She handles pressure very well.

entries.note: andar also means to walk, but leans towards to go about, to be running: el reloj no anda.

ex.es: Caminamos hasta la plaza.
ex.en: We walked to the square.
